title: Scheduler impact notes: prefill/decode split + continuous batching (how it changes apparent kernel wins)
body:
Context
- This is a scratchpad for the FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint. We keep seeing “microbench wins” not showing up end-to-end, or showing up as TTFT regressions in mixed traffic.
- Goal here: explain the scheduler interactions that can mask or invert kernel wins (esp. attention) when we have continuous batching + prefill/decode interleaving + backpressure.
- Audience: runtime scheduling folks + kernel folks + anyone interpreting benchmark matrices.

Glossary / metrics (using our current naming)
- TTFT: time-to-first-token (end-user facing)
- TPOT: time-per-output-token (decode steady state)
- Prefill: prompt processing / KV build (usually heavier per token, larger batchability, often memory-bound depending on model)
- Decode: generating tokens iteratively (sensitive to latency, benefits from stable small batches)
- “Mixed workload”: concurrent requests with ongoing decode while new requests arrive and need prefill
- Continuous batching: we form dynamic batches across requests over time; batch membership changes per step.
- Backpressure: scheduler limits applied when queue depth / in-flight tokens exceeds thresholds; intended to keep latency stable and avoid OOM.

Key point (tl;dr)
Kernel wins are not additive at e2e when:
1) The scheduler shifts the prefill/decode ratio (or changes which stage is on the critical path),
2) Backpressure rules change queueing delay and batch formation, and
3) The new kernel changes step time enough to move us across discrete scheduler regimes (batch window boundaries, prefill vs decode prioritization thresholds).

So: a 20% faster attention kernel in isolation can yield:
- 0% e2e improvement (masked by queueing + prefill dominating),
- A TTFT regression (if decode becomes “cheaper” and we starve prefill longer), or
- Big throughput gain but worse p95 (if the scheduler chooses larger batches and increases tail).

What changed during this sprint that makes the above show up more
- FP8 attention kernels: reduce per-step compute; step time decreases; scheduler has more opportunities to interleave and/or to “wait to batch” (depending on config).
- INT8 matmul paths: speedups can be shape-specific; some regimes change prefill more than decode.
- Instrumentation added (PR-19855): we can now separate prefill time vs decode time vs queueing delay (still imperfect, but enough to see the pattern).

Scheduler regimes (mental model)
I’ve been thinking of this as three discrete regimes rather than a smooth continuum:
A) Low concurrency (queue depth ~0-2):
   - Batches are small, TTFT is dominated by fixed overheads + prefill.
   - Kernel wins show up mostly in TTFT (if prefill improved) or TPOT (if decode improved), but variance is high.

B) “Healthy” concurrency (queue depth moderate, batches ~4-16 depending on model/SKU):
   - Throughput is high, TTFT depends heavily on prefill admission + batch window.
   - Kernel wins can show up as throughput gain, but TTFT might not move unless prefill scheduling is prioritized.

C) Backpressured / saturation (queue depth high, batches push max, memory pressure):
   - Queueing dominates TTFT p95.
   - Any kernel win that increases offered load can increase queue depth unless we change concurrency caps.
   - Sometimes the best “kernel win” increases cost (more tokens admitted) and worsens p95 unless we retune.

Observed patterns from our runs (qualitative)
1) TTFT regressions that are actually scheduler-induced queueing
- In several H100 mixed-workload runs, FP8 attention reduced per-step time but TTFT got worse.
- The breakdown showed:
  - Compute prefill time: slightly better
  - Compute decode time: better
  - Queueing before prefill start: worse (this dominates p95 TTFT)
- Hypothesis: faster decode increases decode slot availability; scheduler keeps more decode “in flight” and prefill is delayed more often (or prefill batches are forced to wait for batch window alignment).
- This matches the Slack thread where TTFT regressed only in the mixed distribution, not in pure prefill or pure decode.

2) Microbench wins not visible because the critical path moved
- Example pattern (not model-specific):
  - INT8 matmul improves prefill by X% at kernel level.
  - But e2e TTFT unchanged because:
    - request admission -> prefill start queueing is now the dominant component, or
    - tokenization / host overhead becomes visible at low concurrency.
- Conclusion: if we don’t control queueing and host overhead, kernel-level delta is a lower bound on what we can realize.

3) Discrete scheduler thresholds cause non-linear effects
- We have knobs like batch window (e.g., microseconds) and caps on in-flight decode/prefill.
- If the new kernel reduces step time below a threshold, we often:
  - form different batches (size/distribution),
  - hit different backpressure thresholds, or
  - change the cadence of “prefill insertion” into decode batches.
- Result: A small kernel change can flip which request is tail.

4) Prefill/decode interleaving can mask a decode-only kernel win
- If we only improve decode, but prefill remains heavy and we interleave, we can end up with:
  - higher throughput in steady state,
  - but TTFT unchanged because prefill is the gating stage for new arrivals.
- For product narratives: decode wins help interactive multi-turn chat (TPOT), but do less for first response latency in mixed arrival patterns.

5) Backpressure makes “throughput wins” look like “latency losses”
- If a kernel win increases total throughput, the system can accept more work, and the queue can grow.
- If backpressure thresholds are too permissive, we can end up with worse tail lat even though GPU is more efficient.
- This is not a kernel regression; it’s a scheduler policy decision.

Concrete knobs that interact with FP8/INT8 changes (list for review)
- batch_window_us (or equivalent):
  - Larger window increases batch sizes and throughput, but increases queueing delay for the first token.
  - Faster kernels reduce step time; same window can effectively be “too large” because we wait to form batches even though we can make progress.

- prefill_vs_decode priority policy:
  - If decode is prioritized too aggressively, TTFT suffers at moderate/high concurrency.
  - If prefill is prioritized too aggressively, TPOT suffers and interactive sessions feel sluggish.
  - Kernel wins that target one stage require revisiting the priority ratio.

- max_decode_inflight / max_prefill_inflight:
  - If decode becomes faster, we can raise max_decode_inflight without hurting, BUT that can starve prefill unless we reserve capacity.

- backpressure thresholds (queue depth, memory watermark, token budget):
  - With faster kernels, we can hit different memory/tokens trajectories (esp. if more requests admitted).
  - Backpressure tuned on baseline kernels may not be stable for FP8 (or may be overly conservative).

- prefill chunking / “prefill slicing” (if applicable to runtime):
  - Splitting prefill into smaller units helps interleaving fairness but adds overhead.
  - If FP8 makes attention cheaper, overhead becomes larger fraction; chunk size may need to increase to realize wins.

Suggested way to interpret benchmark results (so we don’t mislabel kernel changes)
When comparing baseline vs FP8/INT8 at end-to-end level, always break down into:
- Queueing before prefill starts
- Prefill compute time
- Queueing between prefill and first decode step (if any)
- Decode compute time
- Scheduler-induced stalls/backpressure time

If we only look at TTFT/TPOT aggregates we will misattribute scheduler policy shifts to kernel deltas.

Practical measurement guidance (what I want us to do for the matrix runs)
1) Run at least two scheduler configs for each kernel mode
- “Latency-biased” config: smaller batch window, stricter backpressure, slightly higher prefill priority.
- “Throughput-biased” config: larger batch window, looser backpressure.
- Reason: kernel wins can be scheduler-regime dependent; we should show both and decide defaults per SKU.

2) Always include a “no interleaving” sanity mode (if we can)
- Even if we don’t ship it, it isolates kernel effect by stage.
- E.g., run pure prefill-heavy workload and pure decode-heavy workload in addition to mixed.

3) Compare runs at matched offered load AND at matched achieved throughput
- Matched offered load tells “what users see” under same traffic.
- Matched achieved throughput tells “how efficient the system is” holding work done constant.
- Kernel wins may increase throughput; if we only look at offered-load comparisons we may see more queueing (not necessarily a problem, but must be explained).

4) Use queue depth histograms as first-class artifact
- If baseline run has median queue depth 2 and FP8 run has median 8, TTFT comparisons are not apples-to-apples.
- PR-19855 adds queue depth histograms; ensure they’re exported in benchmark artifacts.

Notes from specific anomalies (WIP, leaving breadcrumbs)
- TTFT regression in mixed workload for FP8 attention (H100):
  - Likely interaction: decode speedup + decode priority -> more decode batches -> prefill waits longer -> TTFT p95 up.
  - Action: try increasing prefill priority weight by +10-20% OR reserving prefill slots under high decode occupancy.
  - Cross-ref: Slack eng-runtime/1776419988.

- Cases where INT8 matmul looks “neutral” e2e but microbench says +15-25% on GEMMs:
  - Suspect: we’re bottlenecked on memory movement in attention or on scheduler queueing; GEMM win not on critical path.
  - Action: confirm with stage breakdown and nsys traces for top 3 cases.

- High variance around batch window boundaries:
  - When step time changes, the number of requests coalesced into a batch oscillates; tails vary a lot.
  - Action: consider aligning batch window to step time (or dynamic window based on observed step duration).

Potential policy changes / hypotheses to test (for Sofia + Marcus)
- Add “prefill reservation” under sustained decode:
  - Guarantee at least N prefill microbatches per M decode steps when queue has pending prefill.
  - Expectation: improve TTFT tails in mixed workload; slight TPOT cost.

- Dynamic batch window: shrink window when queueing dominates TTFT
  - Window = f(queue depth, stage mix, target TTFT)
  - Risk: more overhead / less throughput; but might reclaim kernel wins for latency.

- Backpressure tuned per kernel mode
  - FP8 may tolerate slightly higher token budgets before p95 degrades, but we need to validate.
  - Guardrails: keep auto-rollback thresholds in perf canary (see ENG-7426) conservative until tuned.

Operational note (why this matters for canary)
- Perf canary sees production traffic mix, which is often “more mixed” than our synthetic runs.
- A kernel win that looks good on “pure decode” can still cause a canary rollback if TTFT worsens under mixed conditions.
- Recommendation: perf canary dashboards must include stage split and queue depth; otherwise we will keep chasing the wrong thing.

Action items (what I’m doing next)
- [ ] Work with Julian to ensure benchmark artifacts export:
  - prefill_time_ms histogram
  - decode_time_ms histogram
  - prefill_queue_delay_ms histogram
  - queue_depth histogram
  - backpressure_events counter
- [ ] Run quick A/B on one H100 config with:
  - baseline kernels vs FP8 attention
  - prefill priority +10% and batch window -20% (latency-biased)
  - see if TTFT regression disappears while keeping most throughput gain
- [ ] Document the recommended “benchmark interpretation rubric” in methodology page (Claire / Confluence link above)

Open questions / notes to self
- Do we have a reliable way to measure “queueing before prefill start” vs “admission control wait”? Right now we conflate some of it.
- How much of TTFT regression is from CPU-side overhead when decode becomes faster (host scheduling, logging, metric export)? Might need to re-check after PR-19918 (debug logging regression fix).
- For L4 (cost SKU) the scheduler regime may be different (more often saturated). Need separate tuning; don’t assume H100 knobs generalize.

Appendix: quick qualitative decision table (not final)
- If FP8 improves decode a lot but TTFT regresses in mixed:
  -> scheduler change likely (prefill starvation); don’t disable FP8 globally; gate by scheduler config / region; canary with new knobs.

- If INT8 improves prefill but TPOT unchanged:
  -> expected; decode dominates TPOT; claim TTFT/throughput improvements, not TPOT.

- If throughput improves but p95 TTFT worsens at same offered load:
  -> check queue depth shift; consider tightening backpressure or shrinking batch window.
